docs.title: Command-line tool
docs.text:
The otlv executable inspects and structurally validates TLV data, converts it to and from a versioned JSON document, and recovers elements from damaged input, using the public C library through the tlv++ wrapper. Building it requires a C++11 (or newer) compiler; the underlying library itself remains a dependency-free C99 core, so this requirement affects only the CLI target.

otlv --version reports the independently versioned CLI. See versions and releases for version formats and release validation.

docs.title: First inspection
docs.text:
Prerequisite: an installed otlv executable. If you need to build it, follow Build and install below.

otlv dump --format fixed --hex "01 02 48 69"

Expected output:

offset=0 tag=01 length=2 value=4869

This input contains tag 01 with the two Value bytes of Hi. Fixed defaults to one tag byte and one big-endian length byte. The tool requires an explicit format and checks errors; it does not detect the format or infer Value semantics. Next, try commands for files, nested data and validation.

docs.title: Build and install
docs.text:
Build from the standalone opentlv-cli repository:

cmake --preset default
cmake --build --preset default
ctest --preset default
cmake --install build/default --config Release --prefix install-cli

The executable is installed in the standard runtime directory (normally bin). The development guide describes dependencies, workspace and offline builds, presets, installed Core packages and dependency updates. See the installation notes for shared runtime deployment. OPENTLV_CLI_BUILD_TESTS controls CLI regression tests and dependency smoke tests. The CLI requires Core's public C and C++ targets. JSON input and output use the private header-only nlohmann/json dependency.

See C++ and CLI examples for matching parsing, nested writing and Query operations with executable acceptance checks.

The CLI migration regression baseline records the originating source revision, commands, test/fixture ownership and the exact-output comparison procedure for standalone CLI extraction. Its original Core-relative paths describe the historical source layout; see tests for commands in this repository.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
otlv --help
otlv --version
otlv formats
otlv dump --format ber --hex "E1 03 5A 01 12" --tree
otlv dump --format fixed --input sample.bin
otlv dump --format bluetooth-ltv --hex "02 01 06 03 09 48 69"
otlv validate --format der --input sample.der
otlv validate --format ber --input -
otlv dump --format ber --module emv --hex "6F0784050102030405" --pretty --describe
otlv dump --format ber --input capture.hex --input-encoding hex
otlv dump --format ber --module emv --decode --hex "9F0206000000001000"
otlv dump --format ber --module emv --decode --output json --hex "9F0206000000001000"
otlv validate --format ber --module emv --input input.bin
otlv encode --format ber --tag 9F02 --value 000000001000
otlv decode --format ber --module emv --input capture.bin > capture.json
otlv encode --format ber --input capture.json --output-encoding binary --output-file out.bin
otlv dump --format ber --input damaged.bin --recover --tree
otlv validate --format ber --module emv --emv-check dictionary --hex "9F02050000000010"
otlv tag 9F02 --module emv
otlv query 6F/A5/50 --format ber --input card.bin --value
otlv completion bash
cat capture.bin | otlv dump --format ber --output json | jq '.elements'

dump, validate, decode and query require an explicit --format; --input and --hex cannot both be given. --input - (or a bare --input PATH) reads binary stdin, including on Windows, and so does omitting both --input and --hex entirely, letting these commands sit in the middle of a shell pipeline (cat capture.bin | otlv dump --format ber) without an explicit -. encode reads its --tag/--value construction from the command line, but falls back to reading its JSON document from stdin the same way when neither --tag nor --input is given. Command output always goes to stdout and diagnostics to stderr (see Diagnostics and exit codes), so redirecting one never corrupts the other. File input is binary as well by default. Use --input-encoding hex for hex text files or hex text on stdin; --input-encoding binary explicitly selects binary input. Input encoding is never guessed. --hex accepts case-insensitive contiguous hex bytes or whitespace between complete byte pairs; prefixes such as 0x, separators, and incomplete pairs are rejected. An empty hex string or empty file is valid. The same hex syntax applies to files and stdin, including CR/LF between pairs. --max-input-size limits decoded bytes; hex whitespace is discarded as it is read without buffering the encoded text. It does not limit the number of whitespace characters read from a stream.

formats lists only enabled formats: fixed, emv, ber, der, bluetooth-ltv, and nfc-type2. Existing library CMake component options control availability. Unknown or disabled formats fail before reading input. No format detection is performed.

--format fixed defaults to one tag byte and one big-endian length byte, matching tlv_fixed_format_t{{1}, {1, TLV_BYTE_ORDER_BIG_ENDIAN}}. --fixed-tag-size N (any positive byte count), --fixed-length-size N (1 to 8) and --fixed-byte-order big|little configure it; all three require --format fixed and are otherwise rejected as invalid usage. For example:

otlv dump --format fixed --fixed-tag-size 2 --fixed-length-size 1 --hex "0102 03 AABBCC"
otlv encode --format fixed --fixed-tag-size 2 --fixed-length-size 2 --fixed-byte-order little \
    --tag 0102 --value AABBCC

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
The tree example above prints:

offset=0 tag=E1 length=3 value=5A0112
  offset=2 tag=5A length=1 value=12

Offsets are decimal, zero-based absolute positions of tags in the original input. Tags and values are uppercase hexadecimal in wire order. Lengths are decimal value byte counts. Constructed values include their encoded children. Indefinite BER additionally prints encoding=indefinite; its resolved value length and value exclude the enclosing EOC. EOC is never a separate element.

By default, dump prints top-level elements only. --tree prints nested BER/DER elements with two spaces per level; other formats and validate reject this option. Both dump modes still check nested BER/DER structure. Output is deterministic text for inspection, not a versioned serialization format. A malformed input may produce a partial dump before failure.

docs.title: Graphical trees and colors
docs.text:
--pretty implies --tree and prints UTF-8 branches (├──, └──, │) instead of indentation alone. Top-level elements remain separate roots. The original --tree layout remains available.

Tags are cyan when stdout is a supported terminal. Redirected output is colorless by default. NO_COLOR (when present) and TERM=dumb disable automatic color. --force-color emits ANSI sequences even when redirected and overrides those environment settings; --no-color always disables color. These two flags cannot be combined. Windows console mode and UTF-8 output code page are temporarily configured as needed and restored after printing.

docs.title: EMV annotations
docs.text:
dump --format ber --module emv appends a readable name for each known tag. --describe additionally prints the dictionary's value representation and length bounds/step, for example:

offset=0 tag=5A length=1 value=12 name="Primary Account Number (PAN)" description="Decimal digits; dictionary length: 1..10 bytes; step: 1"

Annotations use the built-in EMV Contact Book 3 v4.4 dictionary. Common abbreviations have expanded display labels; other symbolic names are rendered as words. Descriptions are type and length metadata, not a complete prose explanation of every EMV data element or a copy of another parser's dictionary. No value decoding, EMV length enforcement, or transaction validation is added by these presentation options; raw values remain visible.

Known biometric containers select their specific dictionary contexts during BER traversal. Unknown tags remain raw and are labelled unknown in the current context; unknown containers do not cause their descendants to be guessed as ordinary EMV tags. Primitive BER values remain opaque, including EMV elements that describe embedded structures. A standalone context-specific fragment has no enclosing context and begins in the base dictionary unless you select another one with --emv-context NAME (see EMV contexts).

The EMV module must be compiled in. --describe, --decode and --emv-context are accepted by dump and decode (and require --module emv); --output and the color flags are dump-only. --module emv itself is also accepted by validate, where it selects EMV checks instead of annotating output (see below). EMV annotations and checks both require BER, selected with --format ber; the wire format and the module are separate options, so --format der --module emv is an error. Use --format emv --module emv for definite EMV framing; --format ber --module emv retains general BER acceptance.

docs.title: Value decoding
docs.text:
--decode additionally decodes each known tag's value through the OpenTLV codec layer (tlv/codec/) and appends it as decoded="...", for example:

offset=0 tag=9F02 length=6 value=000000001000 name="Amount, Authorised" decoded="1000"

The raw value= field is always present; decoding never replaces it. Only tags with a dictionary entry and a registered codec are decoded - an unknown tag, or a known tag whose value kind carries no codec (raw bytes, text, or a template), is left with no decoded field and is not treated as an error. A value that fails to decode (wrong length, invalid BCD, an undefined enum value, and so on) instead reports decode-error="...", drawn from the codec's own diagnostic; the element itself is still printed, and the command does not fail because of it.

Decoded output favors the codec's own C representation over further interpretation: numeric fields (including currency amounts, which the codec returns as unscaled minor units - see tlv/builtins/emv/emv_codec.h) print as a plain decimal integer, bit flags print as hexadecimal, dates/times print as YYYY-MM-DD/HH:MM:SS (the century of a date is assumed, as the dictionary value itself does not carry one), and enumerated or composite kinds (account type, cryptogram information, biometric type, AFL, CVM Results, Track 2) print a short label or a compact field list. --decode cannot be combined with --pdol, since a DOL entry carries a requested length, not a value.

docs.title: JSON output
docs.text: --output json prints a single JSON document instead of the key=value text above: a top-level object with an elements array, carrying the same information under stable field names (offset, tag, length, indefinite when true, value, name, description, decoded, decode_error) and, for --pdol, (offset, tag, requested_length, name). Fields that do not apply to an element (an unset --describe description, an undecoded value, and so on) are simply omitted rather than set to null. When --tree is set, a constructed BER/DER element carries its children in its own nested elements array instead of a flat list, so the document's shape mirrors the input's structure; without --tree, only top-level elements appear and no element has an elements field. --pretty's graphical tree connectors are a text-mode presentation only and have no effect on --output json. A malformed input may still produce a document containing the elements parsed before the failure, matching the partial-output-on-failure behavior described above; the diagnostic itself is always reported separately, on stderr.

docs.title: JSON export
docs.text:
decode parses the input like dump --tree and prints it as the versioned JSON document: tags and primitive values as hexadecimal strings, constructed elements as nested children arrays, and for BER an explicit length_mode of definite or indefinite:

otlv decode --format ber --hex "E1 05 5A 01 12 5A 00 30 80 04 01 AA 00 00"

{"schema":"opentlv.tlv","version":1,"format":"ber","elements":[{"tag":"E1","length_mode":"definite","children":[{"tag":"5A","value":"12"},{"tag":"5A","value":""}]},{"tag":"30","length_mode":"indefinite","children":[{"tag":"04","value":"AA"}]}]}

decode takes the input, limit and module options of dump (--format, --input/--hex, --input-encoding, --max-*, --module emv, --describe, --decode, --emv-context, --recover) and rejects the text presentation options (--tree, --pretty, colors, --output, --pdol). The whole input is always parsed as a tree, so BER and DER nesting is followed up to --max-depth. A failed export prints nothing on stdout, unlike dump, so a partial document is never mistaken for a complete one. With --module emv each known element carries its dictionary name; unknown tags carry only their raw tag and value.

Offsets are not part of the document. Use dump --output json when you need them.

docs.title: Encoding
docs.text:
encode writes TLV data with the OpenTLV writer for the format chosen by --format, so the format alone determines the tag and length encoding. It has two input modes: one element from --tag/--value, or a whole JSON document from --input.

otlv encode --format ber --tag 9F02 --value 000000001000
otlv encode --format ber --input elements.json
otlv encode --format ber --input - --output-encoding binary --output-file out.bin

9F0206000000001000

For a single element, --format and --tag are required; --value is optional and defaults to an empty value. --tag and --value use the same hex syntax as --hex (case-insensitive, complete byte pairs, optional whitespace between pairs). --value is limited by --max-input-size; a tag longer than 8 bytes, the longest tag any built-in format accepts, is rejected.

--input PATH reads a JSON document instead (- for stdin, read as bytes on Windows too); it cannot be combined with --tag or --value. Omitting both --tag and --input reads the JSON document from stdin as well, the same as --input -. Every length is derived while encoding, children are written inside their parent, and BER elements marked "length_mode":"indefinite" get the 80 length and the end-of-contents octets. Before anything is printed the encoded bytes are read back with the format's reader and checked like otlv validate does, so the output is always accepted by the library reader and structural validator. --max-input-size limits the JSON text and the encoded bytes, --max-depth the nesting of children and --max-elements the number of elements. Nothing about the JSON is guessed: a document that does not follow the schema, names another format than --format, or needs a representation the format lacks (children under default, indefinite length under der) is rejected. The round trip decode then encode preserves element structure and raw primitive values but not the exact bytes of length fields; see Round trip.

Output is uppercase hex followed by a newline by default; --output-encoding binary writes the raw encoded bytes with no newline, including on Windows. --output-file PATH writes the result to a file instead of stdout, and only after the whole document was accepted, so a rejected document leaves no file behind. Either encoding can be read back with otlv dump (--input -, plus --input-encoding hex for the hex form).

Nothing is printed for a rejected input. Malformed hex, an invalid JSON document, unknown or disabled formats, and options encode does not take exit with code 2; encode takes --format, --tag, --value, --input, --output-encoding, --output-file, --max-input-size, --max-depth and --max-elements. An element the writer rejects (an invalid BER tag, or a value too long for fixed) reports otlv: cannot encode element N: <reason> and exits with code 1; N counts elements from zero in document order. Exceeded limits and unreadable or unwritable files exit with code 3.

docs.title: Path queries
docs.text:
query prints the elements addressed by a path of hexadecimal tags, so a script can read one value from nested data without post-processing the whole dump. The path is a positional argument and the input options are the same as for dump.

otlv query 6F/A5/50 --format ber --input card.bin
otlv query 6F/A5/50 --format ber --input card.bin --value
otlv query 6F/A5/50 --format ber --input card.bin --output json

offset=8 tag=50 length=2 value=4142

6F/A5/50 means a top-level 6F, its direct child A5 and that element's direct child 50. Every element reached this way is printed in document order; a tag that occurs several times can therefore produce several lines. Tags are hex in either case, separated by one /; spaces, empty steps and a leading or trailing / are usage errors. This first version supports exact tag paths only, with no wildcards, indexes or recursive search. The syntax and matching come from the library (Path queries), not from the CLI.

  • Text output is one line per match in the format of dump, without nesting.
  • --value prints only the value bytes of each match as one line of hex, an empty line for an empty value.
  • --output json prints {"matches":[...]}; each match has path, offset, tag, length and value. It cannot be combined with --value.
  • A path of more than one tag needs --format ber or --format der, the formats that have nested values; other formats accept one-tag paths.
  • The whole input is still parsed, so damaged data after a match fails the command with exit code 1, and --max-depth, --max-elements and --max-input-size apply as for dump.
  • No match is reported as otlv: no match for query ... with exit code 5, so a script can tell a missing element from invalid data.

docs.title: Full compiled Query and semantic diff
docs.text:
Full expressions can be positional or supplied with --query. Existing exact paths preserve their text/JSON/--value behavior; descendants (//), predicates, sets, typed variables and scalar expressions use the compiled C Query engine through the C++ program/execution facade.

otlv query --query 'count(//50)' --format ber --input capture.bin
otlv query --query '//50[value(.) = $wanted]' --var wanted:bytes=4142 --format ber --input capture.bin
otlv query --query '//50[num(.) > $min]' --var min:int=100 --format ber --input capture.bin --explain
otlv query '//51' --exists --format ber --input capture.bin
otlv diff --format ber --input left.bin --against right.bin --where '//70/5A' --output json

Variable declarations use NAME:int=DECIMAL, NAME:bytes=HEX (even-length hex, including empty) or NAME:string=UTF8. The shell must preserve literal dollar signs; single-quoted examples work in Bash and PowerShell. Variables are bound through native slots, never substituted into Query text. num uses the generic minimal signed big-endian integer provider; bcd uses packed decimal, and text uses UTF-8. Symbolic EMV resolution is enabled with --format emv.

--count and --exists wrap a node expression into a scalar expression. False and zero return exit code 0, as does every successful scalar. Empty node results return 5. Full Query compilation/binding/backend failures return 2 and execution failures return 3; existing V1 input parse failures retain exit code 1. Scalar JSON is { "type": native_result_kind, "value": value }, with integer JSON numbers, booleans, uppercase hex bytes and UTF-8 strings. --value is only for node selections and cannot be combined with JSON.

--backend streaming always uses retained canonical Tree events with explicit --max-elements capacity and rejects D before traversal. It never builds a Document. --backend document selects owning Document materialization explicitly. auto chooses retained streaming for S0-S2 and materializes D. Input is already owned by the CLI; retained payloads borrow that input. The owning C++ convenience and CLI allocate program/workspace/result storage; the C engine does not allocate. The Document backend retains input coordinates, so its matches report the same source offsets as streaming and @offset/@hlen are available in both.

--explain writes JSON to stderr with normalized Query, language/result/level, chosen backend, program/scratch sizing and alignment, capacities, work budget, validation policy and an explicitly unstable internal logical IR. It does not change the normal result output. Full execution drains to structural EOF; Schema or DER semantic validation is not implied. Human/compact/json diagnostics retain native Query byte spans and available resource/source context.

diff requires two files and the Document component. Its selector is compiled once and evaluated on each original complete input. It reports added, removed and changed direct nodes; zero differences succeeds with an empty result. Node correspondence uses ancestor tags and same-tag sibling occurrence, independent of byte offsets. A node selected on either side includes its counterpart. Selected ancestors do not implicitly include excluded descendants. Repeated-tag insertions may shift correspondence. JSON contains a changes array with kind, correspondence path and original left/right primitive content/classification; absent sides and constructed Values are null. This minimal surface does not bind typed variables or provider environments for diff. See Query integration contracts.

docs.title: Tag lookup
docs.text:
tag looks up one BER tag in the OpenTLV EMV dictionary, so the CLI can serve as a quick tag reference. The metadata comes from the native EMV definitions (tlv_emv_find in the base context); the CLI keeps no dictionary of its own.

otlv tag 9F02 --module emv

Tag:         9F02
Name:        Amount Authorised
Type:        Numeric value (binary or decimal BCD, tag-dependent)
Form:        Primitive
Length:      6

The tag is a positional argument in the same hex syntax as --hex, and must be exactly one complete BER tag. --module emv is required. Length step is printed only when the dictionary's permitted lengths advance by more than one byte (for example the AFL). --output json prints one object with tag, module, known and, for known tags, name, symbol, type, constructed, min_length, max_length (omitted when unbounded) and length_step.

A tag with no dictionary entry is a valid result, not malformed data: text output prints Result: Unknown tag in the EMV module (base context), JSON output has "known":false, and the exit code is 0. An invalid or incomplete tag, an unknown module, or any option other than --module and --output exits with code 2.

tags lists every tag in the dictionary (base context), sorted by tag, when you do not know which tag to look up:

otlv tags --module emv --search amount

81      Amount Authorised Binary
9F02    Amount Authorised
9F03    Amount Other
...

--search TEXT keeps only tags whose displayed name contains TEXT (case-insensitive). --output json prints {"module":"emv","tags":[...]} where each element has the same fields as a known tag result. A search with no matches is not an error: it prints nothing (or an empty array) and exits 0. tags accepts only --module, --output and --search; --search is rejected by every other command.

docs.title: PDOL / DOL inspection
docs.text:
Use --pdol to read a raw PDOL value as ordered tag/length pairs:

otlv dump --format ber --pdol --hex "9F02069F1A02" --module emv
otlv validate --format ber --pdol --input pdol.hex --input-encoding hex

Without annotations, the output is:

offset=0 tag=9F02 requested-length=6
offset=3 tag=9F1A requested-length=2

Supply the contents of tag 9F38, not its enclosing TLV header. Ordinary TLV dumping still leaves that value opaque. The same pair representation is used by other EMV DOLs. Tags contain one or two bytes; each requested length is exactly one unsigned byte (0..255), including 80 and FF. No value follows the length. Order and duplicate tags are preserved. This mode neither constructs terminal response data nor checks whether the requested lengths match dictionary bounds.

All existing input sources, decoded-input and element-count limits apply. Empty input succeeds. Missing lengths, malformed tags, and tags longer than two bytes fail with offsets. --tree and --pretty are rejected because a DOL is flat; --max-depth has no effect. BER must be enabled; the EMV dictionary is needed only for optional --module emv annotations.

docs.title: EMV schema validation
docs.text:
validate --format ber --module emv additionally checks the parsed input against tlv_emv_structure_schema (see EMV structural validation): mandatory tags, forbidden/unknown tags, duplicate tags, length bounds, and required nesting for the FCI Template, Application Template, and GPO Response Message Template Format 2. It runs only after the input has parsed as valid BER, only for validate (dump --module emv only annotates tags), and not with --pdol (a DOL's tag/length pairs are not a TLV structure to check against a schema). A schema violation is reported like any other failure, but prefixed with schema to keep it distinguishable from a format/framing error. A missing mandatory tag uses TLV_ERR_SCHEMA with missing detail. The reported Tag comes from the Schema, and its byte position is the enclosing scope end.

$ otlv validate --format ber --module emv --hex "6F00"
otlv: schema TLV_ERR_SCHEMA at byte 2 tag=84: schema constraint violated

The exit code contract is unchanged (1 for a schema violation, 3 for an exceeded limit). Unmodeled top-level tags, such as the Read Record Template, are accepted unchecked; this is not a full EMV transaction or value validator.

docs.title: EMV checks
docs.text:
validate --module emv runs the checks chosen by --emv-check, always on input that has already parsed as valid BER:

--emv-check Checks compact prefix structure (default) The structural schema above. schema dictionary Every element whose tag is in the EMV dictionary, in the context it appears in, has a length the dictionary permits (its bounds and length step). dictionary all structure, then dictionary; the first failure is reported. either

The compact prefix distinguishes the two checks on one line; human and json do the same with structured detail instead: a structural violation carries a path and, for most kinds, a field name, while a dictionary violation carries a dictionary stage.

The dictionary check uses the same lookup and contexts as dump --module emv and the library's tlv_emv_validate_length. It reports the first offending element, labeled dictionary, with exit code 1; see Diagnostics and exit codes for the --diagnostics renderers. In compact form:

$ otlv validate --format ber --module emv --emv-check dictionary --hex "9F02050000000010" --diagnostics compact
otlv: dictionary TLV_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH at byte 0 tag=9F02: invalid length encoding

What runs, and what does not:

  • Tags with no dictionary entry in their context are not errors; they are preserved and left unchecked. The dictionary check does not require a tag to be known, does not check that mandatory tags are present outside the templates the structural schema models, and does not decode or check values (BCD digits, dates, enumerations); --decode shows those diagnostics without failing.
  • Children of a container are looked up in that container's context, and containers the dictionary does not know contribute no context, so their children are unchecked (as they are labelled unknown by dump).
  • Neither check is an EMV kernel, transaction, or cryptographic validation, and cross-tag rules (for example that a tag must agree with another) are out of scope.
  • --emv-check applies to validate only, and not with --pdol.

docs.title: EMV contexts
docs.text:
The dictionary is context dependent: the same tag can mean different things inside different templates (for example 82 is the 2-byte Application Interchange Profile at the top level but a 1-byte Biometric Subtype inside a Biometric Header Template). During a traversal the CLI switches context on known containers such as the Biometric Information Template 7F60. A fragment cut out of such a container has no enclosing element to say which context applies, so select it explicitly with --emv-context NAME, for dump, decode and validate --emv-check dictionary:

Name Context base (default) Ordinary application data. bit Inside 7F60 (Biometric Information Template). bht Inside A1 within 7F60 (Biometric Header Template). bht-format Inside a level-2 A1/A2 within the BHT. bit-group Inside BF4A/BF4B or a terminal group. biometric-counters Inside BF4C. biometric-attempts Inside BF4D. biometric-verification Inside BF4E. 
otlv dump --format ber --module emv --emv-context bht --hex "820101"
otlv validate --format ber --module emv --emv-check dictionary --emv-context bht --hex "82020101"

The first prints the element as Biometric Subtype; the second fails because 82 is 1 byte in that context. Contexts never fall back to the base dictionary. The structural schema models base-context templates only, so --emv-check structure (and all) require the base context; use --emv-check dictionary with any other. --emv-context requires --module emv and cannot be combined with --pdol.

docs.title: Recovery scanning
docs.text:
dump and decode stop at the first damaged byte by default. With --recover they instead resynchronize and keep going. This CLI-owned recovery policy uses the public single-element tlv_read() API: when the element at the current offset cannot be read, or its contents are malformed, it checks each following offset for the next plausible element, and the bytes in between are skipped.

$ otlv dump --format ber --hex "5A0112 0000 5A0134" --recover
offset=0 tag=5A length=1 value=12
skipped offset=3 length=2 error=TLV_ERR_INVALID_TAG error-location=input:point:3
offset=5 tag=5A length=1 value=34
otlv: skipped 2 byte(s) at offset 3: TLV_ERR_INVALID_TAG at byte 3: invalid tag
otlv: output is incomplete: recovery skipped 1 range(s), 2 byte(s) in total
$ echo $?
4
  • Skipped ranges are reported where they occur (skipped offset= length= error= error-location= lines in dump text output), and again on stderr with a summary. error and error-location describe the first failure that made the range unreadable, with the same location as its stderr diagnostic: domain:kind:begin, domain:kind:begin..end for a span, or unknown:unknown when the failure has no location. The location can lie inside or after the range.
  • Incomplete output. In --output json and in decode, the document gains "complete":false and a "skipped" array of objects with offset, length, error, location and message. location has the domain and kind of the failure and, when known, its begin and end, like the location of a JSON diagnostic. An undamaged input under --recover reports "complete":true and an empty array. A recovered decode document is incomplete and is rejected by encode.
  • Exit status 4 means recovery skipped data, so the output is incomplete; it is distinct from 1 (strict failure). Without --recover, or when nothing was skipped, the exit codes are unchanged.
  • Offsets are absolute positions in the input. A recovered element is always reported as a top-level element, even when the scanner found it inside a damaged constructed element.
  • Limits are not damage. --max-input-size, --max-depth and --max-elements still fail the run with exit code 3, and --max-elements counts only the elements that were output.
  • Heuristic. The scanner accepts what looks like a well-formed element (syntactic checks only, no dictionary or schema), so a match is not proof of an original element boundary; damaged bytes can be mistaken for an element, and an element inside a skipped range can be output where a byte-level decoder would have skipped it. Treat recovered output as evidence for inspection, not as a repaired copy.
  • validate stays strict and rejects --recover, as do --pdol and encode. It is the only command whose exit status certifies that the input is valid.

docs.title: Validation and limits
docs.text:
validate is silent on success. Both commands consume all concatenated elements; empty input succeeds and invalid trailing bytes fail. Default, fixed and bluetooth-ltv values are opaque unless a semantic module is selected. BER uses constructed-tag recognition; DER uses the existing structural validator. This does not provide full ASN.1 value validation or canonical SET/SET OF ordering; EMV structural validation is available via --module emv, above. Bluetooth schema and codec validation is available via --module bluetooth.

Option Default Meaning --max-input-size N 16777216 Maximum decoded input bytes (16 MiB) --max-depth N 64 Maximum descendant depth; top-level depth is zero --max-elements N 100000 Maximum visited elements, including hidden descendants

Limits are inclusive nonnegative decimal integers fitting native size_t. Depth is restricted to 0..64. Zero is a real limit, not an unlimited setting. Traversal follows library depth semantics: empty constructed values require no descent. BER indefinite-length resolution also has the library's fixed 64-scope bound. The input is buffered in CLI-owned memory; this does not change the allocation-free library core. Limits constrain accepted input and traversal; they are not a wall-clock timeout or incremental streaming interface.

docs.title: Shell completion
docs.text:
otlv completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/otlv
otlv completion zsh > "${fpath[1]}/_otlv"
otlv completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/otlv.fish
otlv completion powershell >> $PROFILE

completion prints a completion script for bash, zsh, fish or powershell to stdout; install it as shown above (once per shell, or on every prompt for bash/zsh, per that shell's own completion conventions) and restart the shell. The script completes top-level commands, each command's own options, and known option values (--format, --output, --emv-context and so on) from the same tables otlv itself uses, so it reflects this build: only formats enabled at compile time, and EMV/--format fixed options only when those are compiled in. Free-form arguments (--hex, query's path, tag's hex) and file arguments (--input, --output-file) fall back to the shell's own file completion where applicable.

docs.title: Diagnostics and exit codes
docs.text:
Command output goes to stdout; diagnostics go to stderr. --diagnostics NAME selects how a failure is rendered: human (the default), compact, or json. All three describe the same underlying detail, collected independently of how it is presented: the symbolic TLV_ERR_* code, a description, a byte offset, the affected tag when known, and, for a failure inside a constructed element, the hierarchical path of tags enclosing it (dump, validate, decode and query all track this, not just dump). Offsets do not promise the exact corrupted byte.

human prints one field per line:

$ otlv validate --format ber --module emv --hex "6F048402AABB"
otlv: error: invalid length encoding

code: TLV_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH
offset: 0x2 (2)
path: 6F
tag: 84
field: df_name
expected length: 5..16
actual length: 2

compact prints the same detail on one line: this is the CLI's original wording (otlv: schema TLV_ERR_INVALID_LENGTH at byte 2 tag=84: invalid length encoding for the example above), kept for scripts that scrape stderr. json prints a single-line JSON object with the same fields (code, message, offset, tag, path, field, and so on), for scripts that would otherwise have to reparse the human or compact text; a --recover run additionally wraps each skipped range's diagnostic with the skipped_offset/skipped_length of the range it recovered from.

A plain wire-level failure (no --module emv) additionally reports which step failed (tag, length, value or trailer) and, for a value or trailer that does not fit, the declared length versus the bytes actually available:

$ otlv validate --format ber --hex "0402AA"
otlv: error: truncated input

code: TLV_ERR_TRUNCATED
offset: 0x2 (2)
tag: 04
while reading: value
declared length: 2
available: 1

This declared-length/available detail comes from re-reading the failing element on its own once the traversal has located it, bounded to the value it actually sits in (not necessarily the whole input); it is shown whenever that re-read reproduces the original failure exactly. BER and DER's constructed-length handling does not currently surface it back through this path, so a BER/DER value-length overrun shows the step, offset, tag and path, but not the two length lines above; every other format does.

An EMV schema violation (validate --module emv) additionally carries the schema field name and the expected-versus-actual detail for the violated rule (occurrence counts, length bounds, or a primitive/constructed mismatch), computed directly by the schema check, so it is unaffected by that BER limitation. A dictionary-length violation (--emv-check dictionary) is labeled dictionary (see EMV checks) and similarly reports the permitted-versus-actual length and the dictionary field name. Missing mandatory tags use TLV_ERR_SCHEMA with missing detail, the absent tag from the schema, and the enclosing scope end. JSON's anchor identifies this boundary (2), separately from an existing element (1), insertion point (3) or unknown position (0).

Formatting is presentation only, layered on top of the library's structured diagnostics; see Diagnostics for the underlying model.

Code Meaning 0 Success 1 Invalid TLV data, or an element encode cannot write 2 Invalid command, option, hex input, JSON document, or unavailable format 3 I/O failure, allocation failure, or exceeded resource limit 4 --recover skipped damaged data: the output is incomplete 5 query matched no element

Automatic format detection, custom text input syntax, full ASN.1 value validation, EMV kernel behavior, and prebuilt release binaries are outside the scope of the CLI.

docs.title: Bluetooth semantic inspection
docs.text:
With OPENTLV_BLUETOOTH=ON, --module bluetooth adds AD Type names from the public Definition registry to dump and decode. Add --decode to render Flags, Local Names, Tx Power, 16/32/128-bit UUID lists, Service Data and Manufacturer Specific Data through the public value codecs:

otlv dump --format bluetooth-ltv --module bluetooth --decode --hex "020106020AFC0000"
otlv validate --format bluetooth-ltv --module bluetooth --hex "020106020AFC0000"

The dump includes:

offset=0 tag=01 length=1 value=06 name="Flags" decoded="0x06"
offset=3 tag=0A length=1 value=FC name="Tx Power Level" decoded="-4 dBm"

The module accepts trailing zero padding using the public AD container API. Only significant structures are traversed; their offsets still refer to the original input. Embedded zeros remain value bytes. A nonzero byte after padding begins is an error. Without --module bluetooth, bluetooth-ltv remains strict wire inspection, including rejection of zero-length structures.

validate --module bluetooth checks the public AD schema first, then the supported value codecs. Schema and codec failures retain original offsets and raw AD Types in the selected diagnostic format. Unknown AD Types and Company Identifiers are accepted. Company names are annotations from the bundled, non-exhaustive registry; service and manufacturer payloads remain opaque hex.

dump and decode annotate malformed known values with decode_error (decode-error in text) without failing wire inspection. Use validate for semantic validity. Text output escapes Local Name control characters and quotes. --output json on dump retains offset, tag, length and value and adds name and optional decoded or decode_error strings.

decode exports the significant structures using the existing versioned JSON schema. Re-encoding preserves those structures but does not restore container padding. --recover is unsupported with this module; --describe and EMV options require the EMV module.

docs.title: Generate reproducible wire corpora
docs.text:
otlv generate --format ber --seed 42 --count 10000 --output-dir build/property-data/ber

--format, --seed, --count and --output-dir are required. Seed accepts an unsigned 64-bit decimal integer, including zero. Count must be positive and always means complete cases (files in the selected encoding), rather than elements. Case indices start at zero; names are decimal with at least six digits (000000.bin, 000001.bin, and so on). Generation does not read stdin and is silent on success.

Each case represents an independently round-trippable complete TLV stream. The native generator selects the number of elements and nesting per case. The same native generator algorithm version, CLI candidate domain, Format/configuration, limits, seed and case index reproduce identical bytes independently of call order. Retain those settings and the OpenTLV version with a corpus; upgrading can change its candidate domain or generator algorithm.

Limits are --max-elements (default 32, including parents), --max-depth (default 4, roots at zero, at most 64), --max-value-size (default 256 bytes) and --max-case-size (default 4096 bytes). Elements and case size must be positive; Value size and depth may be zero. Nested formats use the requested depth; flat formats use zero. Scratch storage is (effective depth + 1) * max-case-size bytes, plus the owned case result. Cases are generated and written sequentially.

Format Ordered candidate tags Value domain ber, der, emv 04, 80, 30, A0 Primitive arbitrary bytes; constructed child streams fixed Identifier of configured width, every byte 01 Capped to the configured Length capacity bluetooth-ltv 09, FF Capped to 254 bytes nfc-type2 03, FD Capped to 65534 bytes; excludes NULL and Terminator

Fixed accepts the existing --fixed-tag-size, --fixed-length-size and --fixed-byte-order options. Optional formats must be enabled in the build. These are wire corpora: they do not promise Schema, Codec, EMV application, Bluetooth AD or NDEF semantic validity. No property runner is required.

Missing directories are created. Existing target case files are rejected before writing any case, and each file is created exclusively. Unrelated directory contents are retained. A later generation or I/O failure leaves earlier completed files available and reports the failing case; a failed write removes its partial file. Use a fresh directory when retrying. Invalid usage/configuration returns 2; generation failure or I/O/resource failure returns 3. Unsupported formats and impossible limits produce a clear diagnostic.

Choose --output-encoding bin|json. The default is bin; explicit bin behaves identically. Binary mode writes only 000000.bin, 000001.bin, etc. JSON mode writes only 000000.json, 000001.json, etc.; no binary files are written. Each JSON file uses the existing versioned model from otlv decode, including raw primitive Values, constructed children and BER length modes. Use otlv encode --input with the same Format/configuration to reconstruct the corresponding wire case. Both output modes use the same native generated bytes; JSON is decoded and serialized entirely within the CLI. Neither the native C generator nor its tlv++ wrapper depends on JSON or nlohmann/json.

Collision checks apply only to paths of the selected encoding; unrelated files, including those in the other encoding, are retained. Failed writes remove their partial file; earlier complete cases remain available.

docs.title: Documentation origin
docs.text: This guide and the JSON schema were migrated from Core's CLI documentation. Build instructions and repository links now refer to the standalone CLI; command and JSON behavior remain governed by the migration baseline.

docs.title: CLI development
docs.text: This guide covers building and testing otlv from the standalone CLI repository or alongside a Core checkout. Run commands from opentlv-cli unless a step says otherwise. See the command guide for CLI use, contributor guide for formatting and license checks, and release guide for independent versioning and release validation.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• CMake 3.24 or newer.
  • A C compiler and a C++11-capable compiler, plus the generator's build tool. Core requires Clang 18 or newer when using Clang.
  • Python 3.10+ when tests are enabled (the default), and for contributor tools.
  • Git and network access to clone the CLI and fetch dependencies that are not supplied locally. Use a full CLI clone with history and tags; shallow clones are rejected by version generation.

The presets leave the generator to CMake. Windows can use Visual Studio 2022; for Ninja with MSVC, open a developer shell with the compiler environment initialized. Add -G Ninja at the first configure if desired. Use a separate build directory for each generator or compiler.

docs.title: Standalone build
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/OpenTLV/opentlv-cli.git
cd opentlv-cli
cmake --preset default
cmake --build --preset default
ctest --preset default

No separate Core checkout is required. CMake looks for an installed Core package and otherwise downloads the pinned source revision. JSON is resolved separately. To require the pinned sources even when packages are installed, use the Git fallback procedure.

For a single-configuration generator, the executable is build/default/src/otlv (otlv.exe on Windows). Visual Studio puts it in build/default/src/Release/otlv.exe. For example, on PowerShell with Visual Studio:

./build/default/src/Release/otlv.exe dump --format fixed --hex "01 02 48 69"

Expected output:

offset=0 tag=01 length=2 value=4869

docs.title: Local workspace
docs.text:
Recommended sibling layout:

workspace/
  opentlv/
  opentlv-cli/
  opentlv-docs/
  opentlv-workspace/

Only opentlv and opentlv-cli are needed for this build. The documentation portal and VS Code workspace are optional. Starting in an empty workspace directory:

git clone https://github.com/OpenTLV/opentlv.git
git clone https://github.com/OpenTLV/opentlv-cli.git
cd opentlv-cli
cmake --preset workspace
cmake --build --preset workspace
ctest --preset workspace

The workspace preset explicitly selects FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_OPENTLV_CORE=${sourceDir}/../opentlv. CMake does not search for siblings automatically. A missing checkout is an error, with no package or Git fallback. CMake builds that checkout as a dependency without checking out a different revision or updating it. Rebuild the CLI after Core changes; rerun configuration when changing build options.

To select a different checkout, replace the example path:

cmake --preset workspace -DFETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_OPENTLV_CORE=/absolute/path/to/opentlv

A path containing spaces must be quoted as a single argument, for example "-DFETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_OPENTLV_CORE=D:/My Projects/opentlv". The JSON dependency may still need a download; see offline builds.

docs.title: Presets and build configurations
docs.text:
CMakePresets.json defines these configure, build and test presets:

Preset Build directory Core selection Configuration default build/default Installed package, then pinned Git fallback Release workspace build/workspace Explicit sibling ../opentlv Release

List them with cmake --list-presets=all. Both test presets show failures and fail if no tests are found. Neither preset disables tests. Both build and test presets select Release for multi-configuration generators; the configure presets set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release for single-configuration generators.

For debugging with Ninja or Makefiles, use a separate directory and matching configuration throughout. Replace /absolute/path/to/opentlv with your Core checkout's absolute path:

cmake -S . -B build/debug -G Ninja -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug -DFETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_OPENTLV_CORE=/absolute/path/to/opentlv
cmake --build build/debug
ctest --test-dir build/debug --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

For Visual Studio, select the configuration at build and test time:

cmake -S . -B build/debug-vs -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -DFETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_OPENTLV_CORE=/absolute/path/to/opentlv
cmake --build build/debug-vs --config Debug
ctest --test-dir build/debug-vs -C Debug --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

The same pattern supports RelWithDebInfo with generators that provide it. Do not build Debug and then use a test preset that still selects Release. An installed Core package must provide a compatible configuration and runtime; source mode is convenient when developing Core and CLI together.

For persistent personal settings, use the Git-ignored CMakeUserPresets.json. This example adds a local static build and keeps its directory separate:

{
  "version": 5,
  "configurePresets": [
    {
      "name": "local-static",
      "inherits": "workspace",
      "binaryDir": "${sourceDir}/build/local-static",
      "cacheVariables": {
        "OPENTLV_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS": "OFF"
      }
    }
  ],
  "buildPresets": [
    { "name": "local-static", "inherits": "workspace", "configurePreset": "local-static" }
  ],
  "testPresets": [
    { "name": "local-static", "inherits": "workspace", "configurePreset": "local-static" }
  ]
}

Configure, build and test with --preset local-static using the corresponding tools. Do not overwrite an existing user presets file; merge the entries.

docs.title: Dependency resolution
docs.text:
Core selection in cmake/Core.cmake follows this order:

  1. FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_OPENTLV_CORE selects explicit source and bypasses package lookup and Git downloads/updates for Core.
  2. Without that override, FIND_PACKAGE_ARGS CONFIG NAMES OpenTLV enables CMake package discovery for OpenTLVConfig.cmake.
  3. If no package is found, FetchContent downloads the full commit SHA in GIT_TAG and builds it as a dependency.

The selected Core must export OpenTLV::tlv and OpenTLV::tlv++. Packages exporting the old OpenTLV::tlvpp target are incompatible. The numeric Core version alone does not prove compatibility with the public integration from Core #620.

Core source builds use its embedded library defaults. The CLI consumes public targets, headers and APIs; Core implementation code is not copied into CLI.

JSON selection in cmake/Json.cmake is independent: FETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_NLOHMANN_JSON, then an installed 3.11.3 exact nlohmann_json package, then the pinned Git commit. Supply version 3.11.3 when providing a local JSON source tree. This header-only dependency belongs to CLI and does not add a JSON dependency to Core libraries.

docs.title: Installed Core package
docs.text:
Build and install a compatible Core with its C++ facade enabled using Core's public build instructions. Select the installation prefix in a fresh CLI directory:

cmake -S . -B build/package -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/absolute/path/to/core-install
cmake --build build/package --config Release
ctest --test-dir build/package -C Release --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

Alternatively, opentlv_core_DIR can point directly to the directory containing OpenTLVConfig.cmake. FetchContent calls find_package(opentlv_core CONFIG NAMES OpenTLV), so the cache variable uses the dependency name opentlv_core, even though the config file is named OpenTLVConfig.cmake. Multiple installation prefixes can be supplied as one quoted semicolon-separated CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH value, including a JSON prefix. Keep Core and JSON source overrides unset when testing package discovery.

If no package is found, Git fallback is allowed. If a package is found but its required targets or capabilities are missing, configuration or compilation fails; CLI does not silently replace that incompatible package with a Git copy. Installed libraries retain their own configuration: changing Core source-build options in CLI does not rebuild an installed Core.

docs.title: Pinned Git fallback
docs.text:
Use a fresh directory with package lookup disabled and no source overrides:

cmake -S . -B build/pinned -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DFETCHCONTENT_TRY_FIND_PACKAGE_MODE=NEVER
cmake --build build/pinned --config Release
ctest --test-dir build/pinned -C Release --output-on-failure --no-tests=error

This selects the pins from cmake/Core.cmake and cmake/Json.cmake; it needs Git and network access on the first configure. NEVER affects both dependencies. An explicit source override still wins over this setting. The dependency matrix verifies the fetched SHA and target provenance as described in the test guide.

docs.title: Switching modes
docs.text:
Keep separate directories for workspace, package and pinned builds. Switch from local Core to pinned Core by running the pinned procedure above, and back by using the workspace preset. default permits installed packages, so it is not an assertion that the pin was used.

CMake caches source overrides and package locations. Reusing a directory without clearing that configuration can retain the previous dependency mode. Changing a preset name or setting package lookup to NEVER does not remove a cached source override. A fresh directory also avoids generator, compiler and installed-package cache conflicts. Do not edit the fetched _deps checkout to maintain local Core changes; select your own checkout explicitly.

docs.title: Offline builds
docs.text:
Prepare the compiler, build tool, CMake, Python and dependency sources or installed packages before disconnecting. For a source build, supply both Core and nlohmann/json 3.11.3:

cmake --preset workspace -DFETCHCONTENT_SOURCE_DIR_NLOHMANN_JSON=/absolute/path/to/json
cmake --build --preset workspace
ctest --preset workspace

These explicit source overrides work on the first configure without fetching either dependency. CMake does not update their checkouts. Installed packages for both dependencies are another option, provided discovery succeeds. A local Core checkout alone does not prevent a JSON download. Merely setting FETCHCONTENT_FULLY_DISCONNECTED=ON does not provision missing dependencies and is not a replacement for supplying them.

Contributor tooling has separate offline requirements: install its dedicated Python environment and populate pre-commit hook environments while online. See contributor tools. The full dependency matrix intentionally checks real Git fallback and needs network access; its documented --skip-git mode provides partial offline validation only.

docs.title: Supported Core configurations
docs.text:
Setting Effect OPENTLV_CLI_BUILD_TESTS=ON/OFF Enable/disable CLI tests and dependency smoke tests; defaults to ON for standalone builds OPENTLV_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON/OFF Select shared/static Core when building from source OPENTLV_BUILD_CXX=ON Required C++ facade for source builds Core component options Control available formats and optional features in source builds

Reader, Writer, Query with its text frontend, Schema and Codec are required. Document and individual protocol formats may be disabled. The compiler checks the selected Core's public configuration, including installed packages. For example, select static Core with cmake --preset workspace -DOPENTLV_BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF and then build/test that preset. Retain full capabilities for the complete regression and release checks. Reduced builds explicitly skip suites that need unavailable features; those skips do not constitute full release validation.

docs.title: Tests and contributor checks
docs.text:
After building, run ctest --preset default or ctest --preset workspace. CTest includes dependency consumers, command regressions, the frozen baseline, Query conformance, version contracts and release-gate tests. Run all entries for complete coverage; filtering only the integration label omits Query and some tooling tests. See the test guide for detailed coverage, capability skips, direct runners and the shared/static dependency matrix.

For formatting, license metadata and static analysis, follow CONTRIBUTING.md. Keep local results separate from hosted CI evidence. A development build or a local passing test suite does not establish hosted release readiness.

docs.title: Updating the pinned Core revision
docs.text:
1. Select a full, immutable Core commit SHA that supplies the required public targets and capabilities. First develop against an explicit local checkout if changes to Core and CLI must be tested together.
  2. Update GIT_TAG in cmake/Core.cmake. Keep a full SHA, not a moving branch. Update documentation that describes the current dependency and record the change under Unreleased. Historical migration/provenance references must continue to identify their original source revisions.
  3. Use a fresh pinned build to exercise the actual candidate dependency. Local overrides and installed packages can otherwise hide a bad pin.
  4. Run both dependency matrices from the CLI root:
python -B tests/check_core_dependency.py --shared ON
python -B tests/check_core_dependency.py --shared OFF

They build and test successful selection modes and check rejection cases. Do not use --skip-git as evidence that the new Git pin works. Retain the generated logs and summary.json; report which platforms were checked. 5. Run contributor checks and review behavioral differences. Preserve the frozen migration baseline; never regenerate expected observations from the candidate to make a failure pass. Intentional CLI behavior changes require explicit tests and documentation. 6. Before releasing, require the hosted Windows/Linux, shared/static release gate for the exact merged CLI commit. See release validation.

JSON pin updates follow the same validation discipline and also require updating its exact package version and local-source requirements consistently.

docs.title: Development builds and releases
docs.text:
Release is a compiler configuration; it does not make a build an official CLI release. Normal CLI versions derive from this repository's Git history and tags, independently of Core. Local source overrides deliberately allow other Core revisions without changing the CLI version.

The release guide is authoritative for version formats, prereleases, clean candidate builds and the release workflow. The gate checks the exact CLI commit and pinned Core/JSON revisions on both platforms and linkages before creating a new CLI tag. Candidate version overrides are reserved for that workflow. It creates a Git tag only; binary distribution and package-manager publishing are outside this development guide.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check or action Core checkout path is missing Correct the explicit override or clone the sibling before using workspace; no fallback occurs for a bad explicit path Expected the Git pin but a package was selected Use a fresh pinned build with FETCHCONTENT_TRY_FIND_PACKAGE_MODE=NEVER and no source overrides Missing OpenTLV::tlv++ or legacy tlvpp export Select a compatible Core revision/package with the public targets and C++ facade enabled Required Core capability rejected at compile time Enable the required public components in the source build or choose a compatible installed package Offline configure attempts a download Supply both Core and JSON sources/packages; check paths and JSON's exact package version Version generation rejects a shallow clone Obtain complete CLI history and tags, for example with git fetch --unshallow --tags while online CTest cannot find the executable Build first and use the same directory/configuration; Visual Studio Debug needs -C Debug CTest reports no tests Configure with OPENTLV_CLI_BUILD_TESTS=ON, build, and use the correct test directory Runtime cannot load a shared Core library In build trees the CLI prepares Windows DLL placement; for deployment follow the installation notes and provide the installed Core runtime on the platform's library search path Generator/compiler mismatch after reconfiguration Use a fresh directory for the new generator/compiler and dependency mode

CLI owns these documentation sources. The independent OpenTLV Docs infrastructure assembles and publishes documentation; Core owns the native APIs and generic processing semantics.

docs.title: TLV JSON document
docs.text:
otlv decode writes, and otlv encode --input reads, a JSON document that describes a sequence of TLV elements. This page defines that document, its version, and what a round trip through it does and does not preserve. Commands and options are described in the command-line tool guide.

{"schema":"opentlv.tlv","version":1,"format":"ber","elements":[
  {"tag":"E1","length_mode":"definite","children":[
    {"tag":"5A","value":"1234"},
    {"tag":"5A","value":""}]},
  {"tag":"30","length_mode":"indefinite","children":[
    {"tag":"04","value":"AA"}]}]}

decode prints the document on one line, with the members in the order shown below; encode accepts any member order and any whitespace.

docs.title: Document
docs.text:
Member Type Required Meaning schema string yes Always "opentlv.tlv". version integer yes Schema version. This page defines version 1; any other value is rejected. format string on output The wire format (fixed, emv, ber, der, bluetooth-ltv or nfc-type2). Optional on input; when present it must equal --format. elements array yes The top-level elements in wire order. May be empty.

Recovered output (decode --recover) adds complete and skipped; see Recovery scanning. A document with those members is not valid input for encode, because it is incomplete.

docs.title: Elements
docs.text:
Every element is an object with a tag and exactly one of value or children.

Member Type Meaning tag string The tag bytes in wire order as hexadecimal. Required, at least one byte and at most 8 bytes, the longest tag any built-in format accepts. value string A primitive element: its raw value bytes as hexadecimal. The empty string is an empty value. children array A constructed element: its child elements in wire order. An empty array is an empty constructed element. length_mode string BER only, constructed elements only: "definite" or "indefinite". decode always writes it for BER constructed elements. When absent on input, the length is definite. name, description, decoded, decode_error string Informational annotations written by decode --module emv or decode --module bluetooth (description is EMV-only). Ignored by encode.

Rules that follow from this:

  • Hexadecimal strings contain complete byte pairs (0-9, a-f, A-F) and nothing else: no 0x prefix, spaces or separators. decode writes uppercase; encode accepts either.
  • Primitive and constructed elements have different representations. For BER and DER the tag decides which is legal: a tag whose constructed bit is set must use children, any other tag must use value. Formats without constructed elements (fixed, bluetooth-ltv, nfc-type2) accept only value.
  • Order and duplicates are kept. elements and children are arrays, so repeated tags stay repeated and in the same order.
  • Lengths are never stored. They are derived while encoding, from the bytes actually written. A length member is an error.
  • Indefinite length is explicit. "length_mode":"indefinite" writes the 80 length and the end-of-contents octets 0000; it is valid only for BER. DER has no indefinite lengths, so encode --format der rejects it. EOC is never an element of the document.
  • Members other than those listed, duplicate members, values of the wrong JSON type and malformed hexadecimal are rejected.

docs.title: Round trip
docs.text:
The contract for decode followed by encode with the same --format is:

  • the element structure is preserved: the same tags, in the same order, with the same nesting;
  • raw primitive values are preserved byte for byte;
  • BER definite or indefinite length mode of each constructed element is preserved.

Byte-identical output is not promised. Length fields are re-derived in the writer's canonical form, so a non-minimal length such as 5A 81 01 12 re-encodes as 5A 01 12. Input that decode rejects produces no document.

Encoding checks its own output: the bytes are read back with the format's reader and validated with the same structural check as otlv validate under the same limits, so the result is always accepted by that reader.

docs.title: Format constraints
docs.text:
Format value children length_mode fixed, bluetooth-ltv, nfc-type2 yes rejected rejected ber primitive tags constructed tags definite or indefinite der primitive tags constructed tags rejected (indefinite); definite accepted

The writer of the selected format still applies its own rules, so an element can be valid in the document and rejected when encoding: an invalid tag, or a value too long for fixed or bluetooth-ltv.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text: The CLI resource limits apply. --max-input-size bounds the JSON text read and the bytes produced, --max-depth bounds children nesting (top-level elements are at depth zero) and --max-elements bounds the total number of elements. Exceeding one is exit code 3. The document is checked while it is parsed, so an oversized or too deeply nested document is rejected without being built.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A document that is not valid JSON, does not follow this schema, or asks for something the format cannot represent exits with code 2 and a message such as otlv: invalid JSON document: duplicate member "value" or otlv: cannot encode element 1: tag 04 is primitive; use "value" instead of "children". Elements are numbered in document order, depth first, from zero. An element the writer rejects exits with code 1.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: version changes whenever the document changes in a way an older reader would not accept. Because readers reject members they do not know, that includes adding a member. otlv reads and writes exactly the version stated on this page and rejects every other with unsupported JSON schema version.

docs.title: CLI versions and releases
docs.text: OpenTLV CLI has its own Git tags and changelog. Core release timing does not determine CLI versions. The executable remains otlv.

docs.title: Version reporting
docs.text:
otlv --version
OpenTLV CLI 0.1.0

CLI release tags use vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, optionally with a SemVer prerelease such as v0.1.0-rc.1. Numeric identifiers cannot have leading zeroes. Tag build metadata is not supported. The v prefix distinguishes CLI tags from the historical Core convention. Use a checkout with full history and tags. Shallow clones fail explicitly. Each release uses a distinct commit with one CLI version tag; multiple version tags on the same commit are ambiguous and rejected. This also applies when promoting a prerelease to a stable release.

The version is generated from the CLI repository at configure and build time:

Checkout Reported version example Exact clean v0.1.0 tag 0.1.0 Exact clean v0.1.0-rc.1 tag 0.1.0-rc.1 Two commits after v0.1.0 0.1.0-dev.2+g0123456789ab Two commits after v0.1.0-rc.1 0.1.0-rc.1.dev.2+g0123456789ab No CLI tags 0.0.0-dev.<commit-count>+g<sha> Dirty checkout Git metadata ends in .dirty Source export without its own Git repository 0.0.0+unknown

The enclosing project's tags and the Core dependency's tags are never used. Changing Core does not change the CLI version. Rebuilding refreshes metadata; an unchanged generated header does not cause recompilation. Untracked files count as dirty unless ignored. Source exports intentionally do not claim a release version.

Issue #4 intentionally replaces the old otlv <Core-version> output. The historical migration baseline is unchanged: the current test driver compares 153 observations exactly and verifies the version observation against the new contract, including empty stderr, exit zero and no output files.

docs.title: Development checks
docs.text:
Use the development guide for local builds, dependency selection and Core pin updates. The CMake Release configuration controls compiler settings; it does not establish an official CLI release. Normal development builds derive their version from Git even when built in Release.

Pull requests and pushes to main run Windows/MSVC static and Linux/GCC shared builds, pinned dependency selection, all applicable command and tooling tests, pre-commit checks and cppcheck. They upload CTest XML, baseline and Query reports. The quality job records the static analyzer version and logs.

Cppcheck analyzes CLI sources, including conditional command implementations; it uses normal checking depth to keep development checks fast and does not analyze Core or JSON internals. The compiler validates core_requirements.cpp, whose sole purpose is rejecting unsupported Core configurations. Its deliberate #error paths are excluded from cppcheck.

The full dependency-resolution matrix is reserved for release validation. Run it locally when changing dependency selection or runtime linkage, as described in the test guide.

docs.title: Request a release
docs.text:
Merge the intended source, documentation and changelog changes first. Obtain the full 40-character CLI commit SHA. Run CLI release gate from main, supplying that SHA as commit and a new tag such as v0.1.0 as tag. These versions are examples, not an automatic first-release choice.

The workflow:

  1. Verifies that the requested object is exactly that commit and is an ancestor of the trusted workflow revision on main. Rejects malformed/existing tags.
  2. Reads the immutable Core and JSON pins from that commit. The request records those SHAs, CLI SHA, workflow SHA, requested version, run ID and attempt.
  3. Checks out the exact CLI SHA on Windows and Linux, for static and shared Core. Each job fetches and verifies the pinned dependencies, exercises all successful and rejected dependency scenarios, and runs every required test.
  4. Runs the same formatting, license, syntax and static checks on the candidate.
  5. Aggregates all four matrix reports and rejects missing/duplicate scenarios, dirty or mismatched revisions, stale runs, failed tests and unexpected skips.
  6. Uploads the validation report, then creates the requested tag at the tested SHA only when validation and quality jobs succeeded. It never moves a tag.

Candidate builds use OPENTLV_CLI_CANDIDATE_VERSION together with OPENTLV_CLI_CANDIDATE_SHA. CMake accepts this pair only for the exact clean CLI checkout. This lets the workflow test the future release output without creating a tag before validation. Normal builds derive versions from Git. Neither the source nor changelog is rewritten by the workflow.

Validation jobs have read-only repository permissions and checkout credentials are not persisted. Only the final job can create the tag; its gate code comes from the trusted workflow revision. Concurrent requests for a tag are serialized. If another actor creates the tag during validation, create-only publication fails instead of replacing it. Repository tag rules must allow the workflow token to create the requested tag; a policy rejection leaves validation evidence available and does not create a release.

docs.title: Release evidence
docs.text:
• release-request-<attempt>: CLI/Core/JSON/workflow SHAs, version, run ID and attempt.
  • release-evidence-<attempt>-<platform>-<linkage>: per-command logs, CTest XML, configured versions, baseline/Query reports and a matrix summary with compiler identity, architecture, C++ standard and Release configuration.
  • cli-quality-<attempt>: formatting/license and static-analysis logs.
  • release-result-<attempt>: aggregate validation status, required job outcomes, per-matrix summaries and their SHA-256 hashes, build and test counts.

Each successful dependency scenario runs 11 CTest entries, 154 CLI behavior cases (153 original plus the independent version contract), and 338 Query backend checks. The two named external fixture-provider exclusions are recorded explicitly. Release validation covers five successful build modes and six expected configuration rejections per platform/linkage: 20 builds and 220 passing CTest entries across the complete matrix. Counts describe different test layers and must not be added together.

Failure logs are uploaded even when a matrix job fails. Missing evidence cannot be promoted to a passing result. A passing validation report records validation; tag creation is confirmed separately by the workflow's final step and job summary. Download artifacts for durable retention as required by your release process; GitHub's configured artifact retention still applies. Retry with Re-run all jobs or a new dispatch. Evidence from a previous attempt is never reused; rerunning only failed jobs cannot authorize a release.

This workflow creates a Git tag only. Binary archives, package-manager publishing and binary distribution remain outside this migration. Local checks and synthetic gate tests do not establish hosted release readiness; the first real release still needs a successful hosted workflow and tag step.

docs.title: Documentation publication
docs.text:
After a successful CLI release gate, Notify CLI documentation portal sends the exact CLI tag, released commit, gate run ID and attempt to OpenTLV/opentlv-docs. The notifier reads release-result-<attempt> from that run; it does not check out or execute candidate code. The gate's workflow commit may differ from the released CLI commit, and both identities are checked. Notification is a separate workflow: a documentation failure does not undo the CLI tag or change the gate result.

The portal independently verifies the successful gate and its release evidence, resolves the tag and publishes CLI-owned docs/ at https://opentlv.github.io/opentlv-docs/cli/<version>/. CLI documentation has its own version selector and stable alias. Core and Docs version numbers do not determine CLI documentation versions. Prerelease tags are published under their own versions without replacing CLI stable. Existing release snapshots remain unchanged when the portal layout evolves.

Repository setup requires OPENTLV_DOCS_DISPATCH_TOKEN, scoped to dispatching events to OpenTLV/opentlv-docs, and the receiver workflow merged in Docs. Docs also needs OPENTLV_CLI_READ_TOKEN with read access to CLI workflow artifacts and repository metadata to verify the release independently. See the portal publication guide for permissions, activation and provenance checks. The cross-repository credential is available only to the notifier's API step.

If notification fails, rerun Notify CLI documentation portal for the same successful gate; do not rerun the gate to recreate an existing tag. Repeated notifications safely reuse the existing documentation snapshot. Preserve the release evidence artifacts for retries: missing or expired evidence fails verification. Verify the notifier, Docs workflow and published snapshot separately before claiming production documentation publication succeeded.
